extracted_by: hand, T-0293 — the Democrat read, November 1834
note: Vol. I No. 49. The town is on page 3, and every column of it is the Tesseract fallback: the transcription says so at the head of each one, the left edge of each printed column is cut, and the segmenter alternates two physical columns line by line so an advertisement survives as one cut half with a letter list woven through it. The month's better witness for the standing advertisements is 1834-11-12, which sets the same matter legibly; where a reading here rests on that issue the note says so. THE FIRE ORDINANCE OF 3 NOVEMBER 1834 IS THE MONTH'S TOWN NEWS, and this issue is its first printing. The letter-list matter on page 3 columns 3-4 is NOT the Chicago list: it is three out-of-county lists dated 1 October 1834, signed by their own postmasters, and it is recorded unminted (claim c014).

claims.notes: THE TRUSTEES MET ON 3 NOVEMBER 1834 AND THE MEETING PLACE IS THE EXCHANGE. This column keeps only 'held at “the' and then breaks to the next line, where the printed word is lost under the letter list woven through the column; the same ordinance set legibly in 1834-11-12 page 3 column 2 reads 'Exchange,” in said town, on the 3d day of November A. D. 1834', and that is where the supply comes from — a second printing in the same paper, not a guess. It is a DIFFERENT house from the fire ordinance of 13 October, which the trustees held at the Tremont House (1834-10-29 c001). The ordinance itself forbids carrying fire brands or coals from one building to another except in a covered earthen or fire-proof vessel, on a five dollar penalty; its enacting and enforcing clauses are in the 1834-11-12 reading, where they survive whole. The right-hand fragments running down these lines are a post-office letter list, not part of the ordinance — see c014.

claims.notes: THE MONTH'S LETTER-LIST QUESTION, SETTLED HERE. Two complete out-of-county lists stand in this column, each dated 1 October 1834 and each signed by its own postmaster — C. Van Horn and G. W. Laird — and a third, ending 'THOMAS GALAUER, P.M.' at line 2452, runs up from page 3 column 3. NONE OF THEM IS CHICAGO'S. Chicago's postmaster is John S. C. Hogan, who signs the 1 October Chicago list minted from 1834-10-22, and no list in this issue carries his name. Tested by names rather than by signature alone: the 149 names minted from the Chicago list of 1 October contain none of Glen, Griffin, Hall, Hunt, Isaacs, Akin, Terry, Wier, Webb, Sawyer, Spangle, Twaddle or Shepherd, all of which stand in these columns. So these are other towns' lists reprinted, their names are NOT minted as Chicago residents, and the survey behind this ticket — 'October-list matter once more in No 49' — is confirmed as to the matter and corrected as to whose list it is. The office names are cut at the column edge to 'Ge' and 'Paw' and are left with a marked query rather than completed to Geneva and Paw Paw.

claims.notes: THE CHICAGO TEMPERANCE SOCIETY MEETS IN THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, and Philo Carpenter signs the call — the same man whose drug establishment is the anchor of Russell & Clift's store on South Water Street in this month's 1834-11-12. The building is the claim's value: the Presbyterian church is used here as the town's meeting hall, as it is for the library meeting of 1834-11-26. This column is the worst-set in the issue and the hour of the meeting is unrecoverable; it is marked absent. The signature line prints twice, once cut ('P. CARPENT EO') and once as '—_PEARPENTER.', which is the segmenter doubling a line and not two signatures.
